blocks.html: Some words are small, but they do a big job. Please is one of them. We say please when we ask for something.

blocks.name: et-scene

opts.readme: Read the question aloud, then let your child choose. Talk about why.
opts.prompt: Leo wants a cracker. What should Leo say?

choices.text: Leo says, “May I have a cracker, please?”
choices.outcome: Grandma June smiles. Leo asked in a kind way.

choices.text: Leo says, “Give me a cracker!”
choices.outcome: Grandma June feels bossed around. Leo told her instead of asking.

blocks.cap: Asking with please, and telling without it.

blocks.html: When you ask for something, say please, right away, in a friendly voice.
“Give me” is telling. “May I have it, please?” is asking. Asking lets the other person choose to help, and that is kinder.

blocks.title: Let's practice
blocks.q: Mia needs the red crayon. Sam has it. What can Mia say?
steps: Mia wants something, so she asks.
She adds please, in a friendly voice.
She waits for Sam to answer.
blocks.a: “May I use the red crayon, please?”

blocks.name: et-sort

cards.text: May I have some water, please?

cards.why: That is telling, not asking.
A whiny please still sounds like an order.

cards.text: Can I have a turn, please?

cards.why: Ask with please instead.

opts.readme: Read each card aloud. Your child taps a card, then a group.

blocks.cap: Sort the cards: polite or not polite.

blocks.name: et-chart
blocks.cap: A chart to print. Give a star each day your child says please without a reminder.

blocks.html: Saying please only after a grown-up asks, “What do you say?” Or saying it in a whiny, bossy voice. Please works best when you say it first, all by yourself, in a nice voice.

For the grown-up. Model it: say please to your child many times a day. When your child forgets, a quiet look or “Can you ask that another way?” works better than a lecture. Praise the times they remember on their own.
After please comes its partner: thank you. We say thank you when someone gives us something or does something for us.

blocks.name: et-scene

opts.readme: Read the question aloud, then let your child choose. Talk about why.
opts.prompt: Omar holds the door for Ruby. What should Ruby say?

choices.text: Ruby says, “Thanks, Omar!”
choices.outcome: Omar feels good. Ruby noticed his help.

choices.text: Ruby walks through without a word.
choices.outcome: Omar wonders if Ruby even saw him.

blocks.cap: Thank you is for help, not only for presents.

blocks.html: Say thank you for gifts and for help: a door held, milk poured, a crayon picked up.
Thank you tells people, “I noticed what you did for me.” Everyone likes to know their kindness was seen.
Here are some thank-yous to try: “Thanks for helping me.” “Thank you for the snack.” “Thank you for playing with me.”

blocks.title: Let's practice
blocks.q: Dad pours Hana a glass of milk. What does Hana say?
steps: Dad did something for Hana.
It is not a present, but it is still help.
So Hana looks at Dad and says thank you.
blocks.a: “Thank you, Dad!”

blocks.name: et-sort

cards.why: Say thank you first.

cards.text: Thank you for holding the door.

cards.why: Help gets a thank-you too.

opts.readme: Read each card aloud. Your child taps a card, then a group.

blocks.cap: Sort the cards: polite or not polite.

blocks.name: et-chart
blocks.cap: A chart to print. Star each thank-you for help, not just for gifts.

blocks.html: Saying thank you for presents but not for help. A friend who picks up your crayons, or a grown-up who ties your shoe, deserves a thank-you too.
For the grown-up. Narrate your own thank-yous out loud: “Thank you for clearing your plate.” At bedtime, ask, “Who helped you today? Did you thank them?” It builds the habit of noticing.
When you say thank you, you hope the other person hears it. So when someone thanks you, you answer.

blocks.name: et-scene

opts.readme: Read the question aloud, then let your child choose. Talk about why.
opts.prompt: Hana says thank you. What should Sam say?

choices.text: Sam says, “You're welcome!”
choices.outcome: Hana smiles. The kind moment is finished.

choices.text: Sam turns away and says nothing.
choices.outcome: Hana is not sure Sam heard her.

choices.text: Sam says, “Thank you!” back.
choices.outcome: Close! But Sam gave the crayon. The answer to thank you is you're welcome.

blocks.cap: Answering a thank-you.

blocks.html: When someone thanks you, say “You're welcome” or “Glad to help!”
Thank you and you're welcome go together, like a ball thrown and caught. The answer tells the other person, “I heard you, and I was happy to help.”
Other good answers are “Sure!” and “Any time!” Say it with a smile, looking at the person.

blocks.title: Let's practice
blocks.q: Leo helps Grandpa Walt carry a bag. Grandpa says, “Thank you, Leo!” What does Leo say?
steps: Grandpa said thank you.
Leo answers so Grandpa knows he heard.
A short answer is all it takes.
blocks.a: “You're welcome, Grandpa!”

blocks.html: Saying nothing, or saying “thank you” right back. Thank you is said by the person who got help. You're welcome is said by the helper.

For the grown-up. Play “catch”: you say “Thank you,” your child says “You're welcome,” then switch. Toss a soft ball with each line to make it a game. Then thank your child for real help during the day and wait for the answer.
Like please, excuse me is a small, kind word. It helps when we are in someone's way, or when something small goes wrong.

blocks.name: et-scene

opts.readme: Read the question aloud, then let your child choose. Talk about why.
opts.prompt: Two shoppers are in the way. What should Mia do?

choices.text: Mia says, “Excuse me,” and waits for room.
choices.outcome: The shoppers step aside with a smile.

choices.text: Mia pushes between them.
choices.outcome: The shoppers get bumped. That could hurt.

blocks.cap: Excuse me asks for room.

blocks.html: Say excuse me when you need to get past someone, when you bump into someone, or after a burp.
Excuse me says, “I know I am bothering you a little, and I care.” It keeps people from getting pushed or surprised.

blocks.title: Let's practice
blocks.q: Omar is running and bumps into Ruby by accident. What can he say?
steps: A bump is a small accident.
Omar stops running.
He says excuse me, or sorry, and checks on Ruby.
blocks.a: “Oops! Excuse me. Are you okay?”

blocks.name: et-sort

cards.text: Excuse me, may I get by?

cards.why: Say excuse me and wait for room.
That is an order. Excuse me is kinder.

opts.readme: Read each card aloud. Your child taps a card, then a group.

blocks.cap: Sort the cards: polite or not polite.

blocks.html: Thinking excuse me means “I get to talk now.” Saying it to interrupt, then talking right away, is still interrupting. We will practice waiting in Waiting to Talk.

For the grown-up. Set up a “hallway” with two chairs and stand in the gap. Your child practices “Excuse me” and waiting for you to step aside. Then trade places, so they see how nice it feels to be asked.
Sometimes we hurt someone, even by accident. Then we say I'm sorry. A real sorry is more than one quick word.

blocks.name: et-scene

opts.readme: Read the question aloud, then let your child choose. Talk about why.
opts.prompt: Leo knocked over Hana's tower by accident. What should Leo do?

choices.text: Leo looks at Hana and says, “I'm sorry I knocked over your tower. Can I help fix it?”
choices.outcome: Hana feels better. They build it again together.

choices.text: Leo mumbles, “Sorry,” and keeps playing.
choices.outcome: Hana is still sad. A quick sorry did not help much.

blocks.cap: A real sorry names what happened and helps.

blocks.html: A real sorry has three parts: look at the person, say what happened, and try to help.
Saying what happened shows you understand how they feel. Helping makes things better. Then the other person can feel okay again.

blocks.title: Let's practice
blocks.q: Sam spills juice on Mia's drawing. What does a real sorry sound like?
steps: Sam looks at Mia.
He says what happened: “I'm sorry I spilled juice on your drawing.”
He offers to help: “Can I help wipe it up?”
blocks.a: “I'm sorry I spilled juice on your drawing. Can I help wipe it up?”

blocks.name: et-order

items: Say, “I'm sorry I…” and what happened.
opts.readme: Read the steps aloud. Your child taps two steps to swap them, then Check.
opts.title: A real sorry

blocks.cap: Put the three parts of a sorry in order.

blocks.html: A fast “sorry” without looking, or “It was an accident, so it's not my fault.” Accidents can still hurt. Sorry is how we show we care.

For the grown-up. Model it with your own small slips: “I'm sorry I forgot your water bottle. I'll bring it tomorrow.” Avoid forcing an apology in the heat of the moment; wait until your child is calm, then help them find the words.
When you say sorry, you hope your friend will feel better. So when a friend says sorry to you, you can help them too.

blocks.name: et-scene

opts.readme: Read the question aloud, then let your child choose. Talk about why.
say: I'm sorry I took your spot.
opts.prompt: Omar says sorry. What can Mia say?

choices.text: Mia says, “Thank you for saying sorry.”
choices.outcome: Omar feels better, and so does Mia.

choices.text: Mia says, “I'm never playing with you again!”
choices.outcome: Now both friends feel bad.

blocks.cap: A kind answer to a sorry.

blocks.html: When someone says sorry, you can say “Thank you for saying sorry” or “It's okay,” and then let it go.
Saying sorry is hard. A kind answer tells your friend, “I heard you.” Then you can both feel better and play again.

blocks.title: Let's practice
blocks.q: Ruby says sorry for an unkind word. Leo still feels a little sad. What can he say that is kind and true?
steps: Leo does not have to pretend he feels fine.
“Thank you for saying sorry” is kind, and it is true.
He can add how he feels, if he wants to.
blocks.a: “Thank you for saying sorry. I'm still a little sad.”

blocks.html: Staying cross after a friend says sorry. Or thinking you must say “It's okay” when you still feel hurt. “Thank you for saying sorry” is always kind and always true.

For the grown-up. Practice with stuffed animals: one says sorry, your child answers for the other. Let them know it is fine to still feel upset; accepting an apology does not mean the feeling has to vanish.
Words can make people feel happy, like please and thank you do. Words can also hurt. We choose kind ones.

blocks.name: et-scene

opts.readme: Read the question aloud, then let your child choose. Talk about why.
opts.prompt: Hana asks to play. What should Sam say?

choices.text: Sam says, “Sure, come play!”
choices.outcome: Hana joins in. Now there are three friends playing.

choices.text: Sam says, “You can't play.”
choices.outcome: Hana feels left out and walks away.

blocks.cap: Kind words help everyone feel welcome.

blocks.html: Name-calling, teasing about how someone looks, and “You can't play” hurt. Kind words help everyone feel welcome.
Manners are about how other people feel. Kind words make someone's day better. Unkind words can stay with them a long time.
Kind words can be small: “Nice job!” “Want to sit with me?” “I like your idea.” Try to say one kind thing to someone every day.

blocks.title: Let's practice
blocks.q: Omar comes to school with new glasses. What could Leo say?
steps: New things can make people feel shy.
Leo picks words that help Omar feel good.
He says something kind.
blocks.a: “I like your new glasses!”

blocks.name: et-sort

cards.why: Teasing about how someone looks hurts.
Leaving someone out hurts.

cards.text: It's just a joke! (But they are not laughing.)
cards.why: If they are not laughing too, it is not a joke to them.

opts.readme: Read each card aloud. Your child taps a card, then a group.

blocks.cap: Sort the cards: kind or not kind.

blocks.html: Thinking teasing is fine if you are “just joking.” A joke is only a joke when everyone laughs. If the other person is not laughing, stop and say sorry.
For the grown-up. Talk about how words make people feel: happy, proud, sad or left out. At dinner, ask each person for one kind thing they said or heard today.
Every day we meet people: friends, teachers, neighbors, family. A hello is the first kind thing we can give them.

blocks.name: et-scene

opts.readme: Read the question aloud, then let your child choose. Talk about why.
opts.prompt: Ms. Park says good morning. What can Omar do?

choices.text: Omar looks at Ms. Park, smiles, and says, “Good morning!”
choices.outcome: Ms. Park smiles back. What a nice start to the day.

choices.text: Omar gives a small wave and says a quiet “Hi.”
choices.outcome: That works too! A small wave and a quiet hi are a fine hello.

choices.text: Omar walks past and says nothing.
choices.outcome: Ms. Park is not sure Omar heard her.

blocks.cap: Two good ways to say hello, and one that misses.

blocks.html: To say hello: look at the person, smile, and say “Hello” or “Hi.” When someone says hello to you, say it back.
A hello tells people, “I see you, and I am glad you are here.” It makes people feel noticed and welcome.

blocks.title: Let's practice
blocks.q: Leo sees his neighbor, Mr. Diaz, on the sidewalk. Mr. Diaz waves. What can Leo do?
steps: Mr. Diaz said hello with a wave.
Leo answers so Mr. Diaz knows he saw.
He waves back and uses Mr. Diaz's name.
blocks.a: Leo waves and says, “Hi, Mr. Diaz!”

blocks.name: et-chart
blocks.cap: A chart to print. Star each day your child says hello first.

blocks.html: Hiding or looking away when someone says hello. Feeling shy is okay! Nobody has to be loud. A small wave and a quiet “hi” are a fine start, and they get easier with practice.

For the grown-up. Practice at home with “door games”: knock, open, and greet each other. Before a visit, tell your child who they will meet so they can plan their hello. Praise small steps, like a wave, for a shy child.
After learning to say hello, here is good news: there are many polite ways to greet someone, and you may choose one that feels right.

blocks.name: et-scene

opts.readme: Read the question aloud, then let your child choose. Talk about why.
opts.prompt: Hana doesn't feel like a hug today. What can she do?

choices.text: Hana says, “Can I give you a high five instead?”
choices.outcome: Aunt Rosa is happy with a high five.

choices.text: Hana waves and says, “Hi, Aunt Rosa!”
choices.outcome: A wave and a hello are polite too.

choices.text: Hana says, “Ew, no!”
choices.outcome: Aunt Rosa feels hurt. There is a kinder way to say no to a hug.

blocks.cap: Many ways to say hello.

blocks.html: A wave, a hello, a high five or a handshake are all polite. Nobody has to hug.
A greeting is about being friendly. Any of these says, “I'm glad to see you.” Your body belongs to you, so you get to choose.

blocks.title: Let's practice
blocks.q: Grandpa's friend holds out his hand to Sam. What can Sam do?
steps: A handshake is one way to say hello.
Sam can shake hands and say hello.
If he is shy, a wave and a hello are polite too.
blocks.a: Sam shakes hands and says, “Hello. Nice to meet you.”

blocks.name: et-sort

cards.why: You can say no kindly: “Can I wave instead?”
A small wave is easy and kind.

opts.readme: Read each card aloud. Your child taps a card, then a group.

blocks.cap: Sort the cards: polite or not polite.

blocks.html: Thinking you must hug everyone who asks. A wave or a handshake is polite too. Grown-ups can help say so: “Hana likes to wave hello.”
Customs differ. Families and countries greet in different ways: a bow, a kiss on the cheek, a hand on the heart, a handshake. Each is polite where it is used.
For the grown-up. Offer choices before a visit: “Will you wave, high-five or hug Grandma?” Back up your child's choice in the moment, kindly, so relatives understand it is not rudeness.
We start a visit with hello. We end it with goodbye.

blocks.name: et-scene

opts.readme: Read the question aloud, then let your child choose. Talk about why.
opts.prompt: It's time for Ruby to go home from Leo's house. What should she do?

choices.text: Ruby says, “Bye, Leo! Thank you for having me!”
choices.outcome: Leo and his dad smile and wave.

choices.text: Ruby runs out the door without a word.
choices.outcome: Leo wonders if Ruby had a good time.

blocks.cap: A goodbye at the end of a visit.

blocks.html: When you leave, say goodbye to the people you were with. If you were visiting, thank your host too.
A goodbye tells people, “I liked being with you.” Leaving without a word can make them think something went wrong.
Goodbyes can be short. Here are some to try:

blocks.title: Let's practice
blocks.q: Grandma June is leaving after a visit. Mia is playing with blocks. What should Mia do?
steps: Grandma came to see Mia.
Mia stops playing and goes to the door.
She says goodbye and something kind.
blocks.a: Mia says, “Bye, Grandma! Come back soon!”

blocks.html: Running off without a word when it is time to go. Even when you are in a hurry, a quick “Bye! Thanks!” takes one second.
For the grown-up. Give a five-minute warning before leaving so your child has time to finish and say goodbye. On the way out, prompt with a question rather than an order: “Who do we say goodbye to?”
When you say hello, you often use a name. Grown-ups have special ways to be named.

blocks.name: et-scene

opts.readme: Read the question aloud, then let your child choose. Talk about why.
opts.prompt: Leo's new teacher is Grace Park. No one has told him what to call her. What is a good choice?

choices.text: Leo says, “Good morning, Ms. Park.”
choices.outcome: Ms. Park smiles. That is a respectful choice.

choices.text: Leo asks his mom, “What should I call my teacher?”
choices.outcome: Good idea! Asking is always a fine choice.

choices.text: Leo says, “Hey, lady!”
choices.outcome: That is not a respectful way to name a grown-up.

blocks.cap: Naming a grown-up with respect.

blocks.html: Many grown-ups are called Mr., Mrs., Ms. or Miss with their last name, or Dr. for a doctor. When you are not sure, use that, or ask your grown-up.
Using a respectful name shows we care about the person. If a grown-up asks you to use another name, like “Rosa,” using it is polite too.

blocks.title: Let's practice
blocks.q: Sam meets the doctor. Her name is Dr. Ada Bell. What does Sam call her?
steps: She is a doctor.
Doctors are called Dr. and the last name.
Her last name is Bell.
blocks.a: “Dr. Bell”

blocks.name: et-sort

cards.why: Use a name, like Ms. Park.
Use Mr. or Ms. and the last name.

opts.readme: Read each card aloud. Your child taps a card, then a group.

blocks.cap: Sort the cards: respectful or not respectful.

blocks.html: Calling a teacher or a friend's parent by their first name without being invited to. When unsure, use Mr. or Ms. and the last name, or ask your grown-up what to say.

Customs differ. Families, schools and regions do this differently: Mr. or Ms. and the last name, “Miss Ana” with a first name, “Aunt” or “Uncle” for close friends, first names, or “sir” and “ma'am.” Each is polite where it is used.
For the grown-up. Tell your child what to call the adults in their life, and why your family does it that way. Before visiting a new family, check what they prefer.
Good manners mean being kind. But being polite never means you must do something that feels wrong. You learned that you can choose how to say hello. Here is more.

blocks.name: et-scene

opts.readme: Read the question aloud, then let your child choose. Talk about why.
opts.prompt: Something made Sam feel uncomfortable. What should he do?

choices.text: Sam tells Dad, a grown-up he trusts.
say: Thank you for telling me, Sam.
choices.outcome: Dad listens and helps. Telling was the right thing.

choices.text: Sam keeps it to himself because telling feels rude.
choices.outcome: Telling a trusted grown-up is never rude. They are there to help.

blocks.cap: Telling a trusted grown-up.

blocks.html: If anyone makes you feel scared or uncomfortable, it is okay to say no, move away and tell a grown-up you trust.
Manners are for being kind, not for doing things that feel wrong. Grown-ups who love you always want to know when something bothers you.
Who are your trusted grown-ups? Maybe a parent, a grandparent, or your teacher. You can name them with your grown-up today.

blocks.title: Let's practice
blocks.q: Someone keeps tickling Ruby, even after she says stop. What can she do?
steps: Ruby can say no in a strong voice: “Stop!”
She can move away.
She can tell a grown-up she trusts.
blocks.a: Ruby says, “No! Stop!” moves away, and tells her mom.

blocks.html: Worrying that saying no to a grown-up is rude. It is not. Saying no, moving away and telling a trusted grown-up is always okay.

For the grown-up. Keep this calm and brief. Together, name three trusted adults. Let your child practice a strong “No, stop!” in a game. Thank them every time they tell you something, even small things, so telling feels safe.
Playing with friends is fun. It is the most fun when everyone gets a chance. That is what taking turns is for.

blocks.name: et-scene

opts.readme: Read the question aloud, then let your child choose. Talk about why.
opts.prompt: Mia just went down the slide. Sam has not had a turn yet. What should Mia do?

choices.text: Mia says, “Your turn, Sam!”
choices.outcome: Sam slides down. Then Ruby, then Mia again.

choices.text: Mia pushes ahead to go again.
choices.outcome: Sam and Ruby feel skipped. That is not fair.

blocks.cap: Waiting for a turn.

blocks.html: Taking turns means one person goes, then the next, so everyone gets a chance before anyone goes again.
Everyone wants a chance to play. When we take turns, nobody is left out, and the game stays fair and friendly.

blocks.title: Let's practice
blocks.q: Leo, Hana and Omar play a game. Leo goes first, then Hana, then Omar. Who goes after Omar?
steps: Each friend gets one turn.
Leo, then Hana, then Omar have all had a turn.
Now it starts again with Leo.
blocks.a: Leo goes again.

blocks.name: et-order

opts.readme: Read the steps aloud. Your child taps two steps to swap them, then Check.
opts.title: Taking turns

blocks.cap: Put the turns in order.

blocks.name: et-chart
blocks.cap: A chart to print. Star each game where your child waited for a turn.

blocks.html: Taking a second turn before others have had one, or grabbing a toy back before the other person's turn is over. A turn should be long enough to enjoy.
For the grown-up. Use a sand timer or a song for turns with a favorite toy: “When the song ends, it's Sam's turn.” Board games are great practice; say “My turn, your turn” out loud as you play.
Sharing goes with taking turns. Sharing means letting others use something too.

blocks.name: et-scene

opts.readme: Read the question aloud, then let your child choose. Talk about why.
opts.prompt: Omar has a box of crayons. Hana has none. What should Omar do?

choices.text: Omar puts the crayons between them and says, “We can share.”
choices.outcome: Now they can both draw. Omar still has all his crayons.

choices.text: Omar hides the crayons.
choices.outcome: Hana cannot draw, and she feels left out.

blocks.cap: Sharing so everyone can have fun.

blocks.html: Sharing can mean taking turns, playing together, or letting someone use something for a while. It is still yours.
When we share, more people get to have fun. Sharing tells a friend, “I want you to enjoy this too.”
You can say: “Let's use it together.” “You can have a turn when I'm done.” “Do you want some?”

blocks.title: Let's practice
blocks.q: Ruby has one special teddy bear. Leo is coming over. What can Ruby do?
steps: Some special things are hard to share. That is okay.
Ruby can put the bear away before Leo comes.
Then she shares the other toys happily.
blocks.a: Ruby puts her bear away and shares her other toys.

blocks.name: et-sort

cards.text: You can have a turn, then me.

cards.why: Sharing can mean taking turns.
Putting away one special thing is fine; hiding everything leaves a friend out.

opts.readme: Read each card aloud. Your child taps a card, then a group.

blocks.cap: Sort the cards: sharing or not sharing.

blocks.name: et-chart
blocks.cap: A chart to print. Star the days your child shares.

blocks.html: Thinking sharing means giving a toy away for good. Sharing can mean taking turns or playing together. And it is fine to put away one special thing before a friend comes.
For the grown-up. Before a playdate, let your child choose one or two special toys to put away. Praise sharing when you see it: “You let Hana use the blue one. She looked so happy.”
Games are better with friends. When you want to join a game, or when someone wants to join yours, there are kind words to use. They build on sharing.

blocks.name: et-scene

opts.readme: Read the question aloud, then let your child choose. Talk about why.
opts.prompt: Sam asks to play. What should Leo say?

choices.text: Leo says, “Sure, come play!”
choices.outcome: Sam joins in. The game is even more fun with three.

choices.text: Leo says, “You can't play.”
choices.outcome: Sam feels left out and walks away.

blocks.cap: Asking to join, and letting someone in.

blocks.html: To join, ask “Can I play too?” When someone asks you, say “Sure, come play!”
Asking first lets the players make room. Saying yes helps everyone feel welcome. Nobody likes to be left out.
Sometimes friends say, “We are almost done. You can play next round!” That is a kind answer too. Wait a little, and your turn will come.

blocks.title: Let's practice
blocks.q: Mia wants to join a game of tag. Hana and Omar are already playing. What should Mia do?
steps: Mia walks over.
She waits for a moment when they can hear her.
She asks.
blocks.a: Mia asks, “Can I play too?”

blocks.html: Barging into a game without asking, or telling someone “You can't play.” Asking first, and letting others in, keep a game friendly.
For the grown-up. Role-play at home: you play with blocks, and your child practices asking to join. Then switch, and you ask. Talk about how it feels to hear “Sure!” and how it feels to hear “No.”
Some things belong to us. Some belong to other people. Just like with sharing, we think about the owner.

blocks.name: et-scene

opts.readme: Read the question aloud, then let your child choose. Talk about why.
opts.prompt: Mia's crayons are on the table. Nobody is using them. What should Hana do?

choices.text: Hana asks, “Mia, may I use your crayons?”
choices.outcome: Mia says yes. Hana asked first.

choices.text: Hana takes them, because nobody is using them.
choices.outcome: Mia is upset. They are still her crayons.

blocks.cap: Asking before you borrow.

blocks.html: Ask before you use something that belongs to someone else. Take care of it. Give it back.
The owner gets to choose. Asking shows respect for them and for their things.
Asking first sounds like this: “May I use your book?” “Can I borrow your ball? I'll give it back.” When the owner says no, that is okay too. It is still theirs.

blocks.title: Let's practice
blocks.q: Leo borrowed Omar's ball. Now it is time to go home. What should Leo do?
steps: The ball belongs to Omar.
Leo took care of it while he played.
Now he gives it back and says thanks.
blocks.a: Leo gives the ball back: “Thanks for sharing, Omar!”

blocks.name: et-sort

cards.text: Can I borrow your book? I'll give it back.
(Takes a toy that is not being used.)
cards.why: Ask first, even if it looks free.
Borrowed things go back to the owner.

opts.readme: Read each card aloud. Your child taps a card, then a group.

blocks.cap: Sort the cards: polite or not polite.

blocks.html: Taking a toy or crayon because no one is using it right now. If it is not yours, ask first, even if it looks free.
For the grown-up. Ask your child before you borrow their things too: “May I use your scissors?” It shows the rule works for everyone, grown-ups included.
When we play games, someone wins and someone loses. After learning about taking turns, here is how to be a good sport either way.

blocks.name: et-scene

opts.readme: Read the question aloud, then let your child choose. Talk about why.
opts.prompt: Omar wins the race. What should he say?

choices.text: Omar says, “Good race, Ruby! Want to go again?”
choices.outcome: Ruby smiles. They race again.

choices.text: Omar shouts, “I win! You're so slow!”
choices.outcome: Ruby feels bad and doesn't want to play anymore.

blocks.cap: A good winner.

blocks.html: A good winner does not brag. A good loser does not pout. Both say “Good game!” and play again.
Games are for fun. If winning makes a friend feel bad, or losing makes us quit, the fun stops for everyone.
It is fine to feel sad when you lose, and happy when you win. Good sports feel their feelings and still say kind words.

blocks.title: Let's practice
blocks.q: Sam loses a board game to Hana. He feels a little sad. What can he do?
steps: It is okay to feel sad.
Sam takes a deep breath.
He tells Hana “Good game” and asks to play again.
blocks.a: Sam says, “Good game, Hana! Can we play again?”

blocks.name: et-sort

cards.why: Bragging makes the other person feel bad.
Quitting spoils the game for everyone.
Blaming is not fair. Say good game.

opts.readme: Read each card aloud. Your child taps a card, then a group.

blocks.cap: Sort the cards: good sport or not.

blocks.html: Cheering about winning in a way that makes the other child feel bad, or quitting a game when you start to lose.
For the grown-up. Play short games and lose on purpose sometimes, showing how: “Oh, I lost! Good game. Let's play again.” Praise good-sport moments more than wins.
Being a good sport means not getting friends in trouble over small things. But some things a grown-up must know. How can you tell the difference?

blocks.name: et-scene

opts.readme: Read the question aloud, then let your child choose. Talk about why.
opts.prompt: Leo fell off the slide and is crying. Should Ruby tell Ms. Park?

choices.text: Yes. Ruby tells Ms. Park right away.
choices.outcome: Ms. Park goes to help Leo. Telling was the right thing.

choices.text: No. Ruby does not want to tattle.
choices.outcome: Someone is hurt. That is telling, not tattling.

blocks.cap: Telling a grown-up when someone is hurt.

blocks.html: Telling is getting help when someone is hurt, in danger, or being unkind. Tattling is trying to get someone in trouble over something small.
Grown-ups need to know when someone could get hurt, so they can help. Small things, like a purple sky in a drawing, are not a problem.
Ask yourself one question: Could someone get hurt? If the answer is yes, or if someone is being unkind, tell a grown-up right away.

blocks.title: Let's practice
blocks.q: Omar is climbing the fence near the busy street. Should Hana tell a grown-up?
steps: Could someone get hurt? Yes.
So this is telling, not tattling.
Hana gets a grown-up right away.
blocks.a: Yes. Hana tells a grown-up.

blocks.name: et-sort

cards.text: Someone is climbing near the street.
A friend colored the sky purple.
cards.why: That is small. No one is hurt.

cards.text: A friend has a sticker on her hand.
cards.why: That is small. Let it go.

opts.readme: Read each card aloud. Your child taps a card, then a group.

blocks.cap: Sort the cards: tell a grown-up, or let it go.

blocks.html: Stopping telling grown-ups about real problems because someone said “Don't tattle.” If someone could get hurt, always tell.
For the grown-up. Use the question “Is someone hurt, in danger, or being unkind?” When your child reports something small, help them solve it themselves; when it is real, thank them for telling.
Talking is only half of a conversation. The other half is listening. Good listeners use their eyes, their bodies and their ears.

blocks.name: et-scene

opts.readme: Read the question aloud, then let your child choose. Talk about why.
opts.prompt: Ms. Park is reading a story. How can Hana listen well?

choices.text: Hana looks at Ms. Park and keeps her body still.
choices.outcome: Hana hears the whole story, and Ms. Park can tell she cares.

choices.text: Hana plays with a toy and then asks, “What?”
choices.outcome: Hana missed the story. Looking at the speaker helps you hear.

blocks.cap: Listening with eyes, body and ears.

blocks.html: To listen well: look at the person talking, keep your body still, and wait until they finish.
When you look at someone, it is easier to hear and understand them. It also shows them you care about what they say.
Here is a trick to remember: eyes on the speaker, body still, ears open, mouth waiting.

blocks.title: Let's practice
blocks.q: Grandpa Walt is telling Sam about a fishing trip. Sam is building with blocks. What should Sam do?
steps: Grandpa is talking to Sam.
Sam puts the blocks down.
He looks at Grandpa and listens until he is done.
blocks.a: Sam stops, looks at Grandpa, and listens.

blocks.name: et-chart
blocks.cap: A chart to print. Star each day of good listening.

blocks.html: Looking around or playing while someone talks, then saying “What?” Looking at the speaker helps you hear, and it shows you care.
For the grown-up. Get down to your child's eye level when you talk, and listen the same way when they talk to you. Play “Simon says” or tell a short story and ask one question about it afterward.
Sometimes you want to talk while grown-ups are talking. You know how to listen and how to say excuse me. Now put them together.

blocks.name: et-scene

opts.readme: Read the question aloud, then let your child choose. Talk about why.
opts.prompt: Mom is talking with a friend. Leo wants a snack. What should he do?

choices.text: Leo waits for a pause, says, “Excuse me,” and waits.
choices.outcome: Mom finishes her sentence and turns to Leo.

choices.text: Leo says, “Excuse me!” and starts talking right away.
choices.outcome: Leo said excuse me, but then he didn't wait.

blocks.cap: Excuse me, then wait.

blocks.html: When grown-ups are talking, wait for a pause, say “Excuse me,” and wait to be called on, unless something is wrong.
Waiting lets people finish what they are saying. Then they can turn and really listen to you.

blocks.title: Let's practice
blocks.q: Dad is talking with Mr. Diaz. Ruby's friend falls and gets hurt. What should Ruby do?
steps: Someone is hurt. That is something wrong.
Ruby does not wait for a pause.
She tells Dad right away.
blocks.a: “Excuse me, Dad! Omar is hurt!”

blocks.name: et-order

opts.readme: Read the steps aloud. Your child taps two steps to swap them, then Check.
opts.title: Waiting to talk

blocks.cap: Put the steps in order.

blocks.html: Thinking excuse me lets you talk right away. Say it once, then wait. If someone is hurt, it is right to interrupt.

Customs differ. Some families use a quiet signal: the child puts a hand on the grown-up's arm, and the grown-up puts a hand on top to say, “I know. One minute.” Either way, waiting is the polite part.
For the grown-up. When your child waits well, respond quickly so waiting pays off. Agree on your family's signal ahead of time, and practice it during a phone call.
Our voices can be soft or loud. Good listeners know that the place decides how loud we should be.

blocks.name: et-scene

opts.readme: Read the question aloud, then let your child choose. Talk about why.
opts.prompt: Mia wants to show Omar a funny page. How should she talk?

choices.text: Mia whispers, “Look at this!”
choices.outcome: Omar giggles quietly. Everyone keeps reading.

choices.text: Mia shouts, “OMAR! LOOK!”
choices.outcome: Everyone looks up. The library is for quiet voices.

blocks.cap: An inside voice in the library.

blocks.html: Use a soft inside voice in homes, classrooms, stores and libraries. Save loud outside voices for the playground.
Inside, people are close together. Loud voices bother people who are reading, working or resting. Outside, there is room for big voices.
Think of your voice like a radio with a knob. Turn it down for inside places. Turn it up a little for outside play.

blocks.title: Let's practice
blocks.q: Sam is on the playground. He wants Hana to come over. Is a loud voice okay?
steps: The playground is an outside place.
People are running and playing.
A loud call is fine there.
blocks.a: Yes. Sam can call, “Over here, Hana!”

blocks.name: et-sort

opts.readme: Read each card aloud. Your child taps a card, then a group.

blocks.cap: Sort the places: inside voice or outside voice.

blocks.name: et-chart
blocks.cap: A chart to print. Star each day your child chooses the right voice.

blocks.html: Using a playground voice indoors when you are excited. Being excited is great! But the place decides how loud we should be.
For the grown-up. Make a “voice meter” together: 1 is a whisper, 2 an inside voice, 3 a playground voice. Before going somewhere, ask, “What number is this place?”
A phone call is like saying hello, but the other person cannot see you. They can only hear you.

blocks.name: et-scene

opts.readme: Read the question aloud, then let your child choose. Talk about why.
opts.prompt: The caller asks for Ruby's dad. What should Ruby do?

choices.text: Ruby says, “Please wait,” and goes to get Dad.
choices.outcome: The caller waits, and Dad comes to the phone.

choices.text: Ruby yells, “DAD! PHONE!” right into the phone.
choices.outcome: Ouch! That was loud in the caller's ear.

blocks.cap: Answering the phone kindly.

blocks.html: Answer with “Hello?” and speak clearly. If the call is for a grown-up, say “Please wait,” and go get them.
On the phone, words are all the caller has. Clear words and “please wait” tell them what is happening.

blocks.title: Let's practice
blocks.q: The phone rings. Omar answers. The caller asks for his mom. What does Omar do?
steps: Omar says hello clearly.
The call is for Mom, so he says, “Please wait. I'll get her.”
He sets the phone down gently and walks to get her.
blocks.a: Omar says, “Please wait,” and walks to get Mom.

blocks.name: et-order

items: Listen to who the caller wants.
Set the phone down gently and go get the grown-up.
opts.readme: Read the steps aloud. Your child taps two steps to swap them, then Check.
opts.title: Answering the phone

blocks.cap: Put the steps in order.

blocks.html: Shouting for a parent while still holding the phone to your mouth, or putting the phone down without a word. Say “Please wait,” then walk to get them.

Customs differ. Families have their own rules about who may answer the phone. Some children answer; some let a grown-up answer. Follow your family's rule. If you don't know what to say on a call, get a grown-up.
For the grown-up. Practice with a toy phone: ring, answer, “Please wait,” and fetch. Decide your family's rule for answering and for what to do when a call is not for them, and say it simply.
Before we eat, we get our hands ready. Clean hands are the first table manner.

blocks.name: et-scene

opts.readme: Read the question aloud, then let your child choose. Talk about why.
opts.prompt: Leo was playing in the sandbox. What should he do first?

choices.text: Leo washes his hands with soap.
choices.outcome: Clean hands, ready to eat!

choices.text: Leo splashes his hands with water for one second.
choices.outcome: Almost! Without soap and a good scrub, the sand and dirt stay on.

blocks.cap: Getting ready for dinner.

blocks.html: Wash with water and soap, scrub all over, rinse, then dry.
Hands touch everything. Washing keeps dirt off our food, and it is kind to the people we eat with and pass food to.
Wash before you eat, after you use the bathroom, after you play outside, and after you blow your nose or cough into your hands.

blocks.title: Let's practice
blocks.q: Hana comes in from the park. It is snack time. What does she do?
steps: She wets her hands and adds soap.
She scrubs the fronts, the backs, between her fingers and under her nails, for about as long as it takes to hum “Happy Birthday” twice.
She rinses and dries.
blocks.a: Hana washes with soap, scrubs, rinses and dries. Now she can eat.

blocks.name: et-order

items: Scrub fronts, backs and between your fingers.
opts.readme: Read the steps aloud. Your child taps two steps to swap them, then Check.
opts.title: Washing hands

blocks.cap: Put the hand-washing steps in order.

blocks.name: et-chart
blocks.cap: A table manners chart to print.

blocks.html: Rinsing for one second without soap. Soap and a good scrub are what clean hands. Then rinse and dry.
For the grown-up. Wash hands together before meals so it becomes a routine, not a reminder. A step stool and soap your child can reach make it easier to do alone.

sources.name: CDC, “Handwashing: Clean Hands Save Lives”: when and how to wash your hands

blocks.html: Your hands are clean. Now it is time to sit down to eat. How we sit at the table matters too.

blocks.name: et-scene

opts.readme: Read the question aloud, then let your child choose. Talk about why.
opts.prompt: Ruby wants to reach the bread. What should she do?

choices.text: Ruby stays on her bottom and asks, “Please pass the bread.”
choices.outcome: Grandma passes it. Ruby stays safe in her seat.

choices.text: Ruby kneels on her chair to reach.
choices.outcome: The chair wobbles. Sitting on your bottom is safer.

blocks.cap: Staying seated at the table.

blocks.html: Sit on your bottom, with your chair pulled in and feet down. Stay in your seat until the meal is over.
Sitting well is safe: chairs stay on the floor and cups stay on the table. Staying in your seat keeps your family company.

blocks.title: Let's practice
blocks.q: Omar has eaten some dinner. He wants to look out the window. What should he do?
steps: The meal is not over yet.
Getting up and down leaves the others.
Omar stays in his seat and talks with his family.
blocks.a: Omar stays seated until the meal is over.

blocks.name: et-posture

opts.readme: Ask your child which one is sitting well, and why.

blocks.cap: Which one is sitting well at the table? Tap it, then Check.

blocks.name: et-chart
blocks.cap: A table manners chart to print.

blocks.html: Kneeling on the chair, tipping back on two legs, or wandering away and coming back. Staying seated is a way of keeping others company.

For the grown-up. A chair your child's feet can rest on (or a box under the feet) makes sitting still much easier. Keep meals short for young children, and end the meal when they are done rather than making them wait a long time.
When you sit down at the table, the first thing to do is find your napkin.

blocks.name: et-scene

opts.readme: Read the question aloud, then let your child choose. Talk about why.
opts.prompt: Sam has sauce on his fingers. What should he do?

choices.text: Sam wipes them on his napkin.
choices.outcome: Clean fingers and a clean shirt.

choices.text: Sam wipes them on his shirt.
choices.outcome: Oops! Now the shirt has sauce on it.

blocks.cap: The napkin is for messy fingers.

blocks.html: Put your napkin on your lap when you sit down. Use it to wipe your mouth and fingers.
The napkin waits on your lap, ready for spills and messy fingers. It keeps your clothes, the table and your hands clean.
When the meal is over, leave your napkin loosely on the table, next to your plate. A grown-up will show you where it goes at your house.

blocks.title: Let's practice
blocks.q: Mia sits down to eat. Her napkin is next to her plate. What should she do?
steps: The napkin is next to the plate, on the left.
Mia unfolds it.
She lays it on her lap.
blocks.a: Mia puts her napkin on her lap.

blocks.name: et-setting
blocks.cap: A simple place setting. The napkin is on the left. When you sit down, it goes on your lap.

blocks.name: et-chart
blocks.cap: A table manners chart to print.

blocks.html: Wiping hands on clothes, or using a sleeve. The napkin is there so we never have to.
For the grown-up. Give your child their own napkin at every meal, even snacks, so it becomes automatic. Cloth napkins are easy to grab and fun to fold.
You are sitting at the table, and your plate is full. It smells so good! But wait…

blocks.name: et-scene

opts.readme: Read the question aloud, then let your child choose. Talk about why.
opts.prompt: Hana has food, but Grandpa and Leo don't yet. What should Hana do?

choices.text: Hana waits until everyone has food.
choices.outcome: Soon everyone is served, and they start together.

choices.text: Hana starts eating fast.
choices.outcome: Leo still has an empty plate. Eating together means starting together.

blocks.cap: Waiting until everyone is served.

blocks.html: Wait to start eating until everyone has food, or until the cook or a grown-up says to begin.
A meal together is about being together. Waiting shows we are eating with our family, not just eating.

blocks.title: Let's practice
blocks.q: Everyone has food. Mom, who cooked, says, “Let's eat!” What can Sam do?
steps: Everyone is served.
The cook said to begin.
Now Sam can start.
blocks.a: Sam starts to eat.

blocks.html: Starting to eat the moment your plate arrives. Wait until everyone has food, or until a grown-up says to begin.

Customs differ. Families start meals in different ways. Some say a few words or a blessing; some say “Let's eat!”; some just begin together. When you eat at a friend's house, wait quietly and follow their family's way.

For the grown-up. Choose a simple signal that starts your family's meal, and use it every time. If a young child can't wait long, serve them last-but-quickly or let them help bring dishes so the wait is short.
Now it is time to eat! How we chew is a table manner too. It goes with sitting well.

blocks.name: et-scene

opts.readme: Read the question aloud, then let your child choose. Talk about why.
opts.prompt: Mia has food in her mouth and wants to tell a story. What should she do?

choices.text: Mia finishes chewing, swallows, then tells the story.
choices.outcome: Everyone hears the story, and no food falls out.

choices.text: Mia talks with her mouth full.
choices.outcome: Nobody can understand her, and a crumb flies out!

blocks.cap: Swallow first, then talk.

blocks.html: Take small bites, chew with your lips closed, and swallow before you talk.
Nobody wants to see chewed food. Closed lips and empty mouths are kind to everyone at the table, and they help people understand you.
Here is a quick check: if someone looks at you while you chew, can they see your food? If your lips are closed, they can't.

blocks.title: Let's practice
blocks.q: Grandma asks Leo a question while he is chewing. What does he do?
steps: Leo keeps his lips closed.
He can nod or hold up one finger to say “one moment.”
He swallows, then answers.
blocks.a: Leo finishes chewing, then answers Grandma.

blocks.name: et-sort

cards.why: Close your lips.
Swallow first. The story will wait.
Small bites are easier to chew.

opts.readme: Read each card aloud. Your child taps a card, then a group.

blocks.cap: Sort the cards: polite or not polite.

blocks.name: et-chart
blocks.cap: A table manners chart to print.

blocks.html: Talking with a full mouth because you are excited to say something. Swallow first; the story will wait.
For the grown-up. Cut food into small pieces for little mouths. Use a friendly code word or gesture (a finger to your own lips) instead of correcting your child in front of others.
You know how to say please and how to chew politely. What about food that is far away?

blocks.name: et-scene

opts.readme: Read the question aloud, then let your child choose. Talk about why.
opts.prompt: The peas are far from Omar. What should he do?

choices.text: Omar asks, “Please pass the peas.”
choices.outcome: Mom passes the peas. No cups get knocked over.

choices.text: Omar stretches across Ruby's plate to grab them.
choices.outcome: Omar's arm is in Ruby's food, and her cup wobbles!

blocks.cap: Asking instead of reaching.

blocks.html: If something is out of reach, ask “Please pass the peas” instead of reaching across someone's plate.
Reaching across the table can knock over cups and puts arms in other people's food. Asking is safer, and it is kinder to your neighbors.
When you pass something, hold it carefully with two hands, and hand it to the person, not over their food. Then you can say, “Here you go.”

blocks.title: Let's practice
blocks.q: Leo asks Hana, “Please pass the bread.” What should Hana do?
steps: Leo asked kindly.
Hana picks up the bread basket carefully.
She hands it to Leo.
blocks.a: Hana passes it: “Here you go.”

blocks.name: et-sort

cards.text: Could you please pass the salt?

cards.why: Ask instead of reaching.
Stay seated and ask.

opts.readme: Read each card aloud. Your child taps a card, then a group.

blocks.cap: Sort the cards: polite or not polite.

blocks.html: Stretching across the table or standing up to grab a dish. Asking is safer for the cups and kinder to neighbors.
For the grown-up. Serve family-style sometimes, with bowls on the table, so your child gets real practice asking and passing. Small, light bowls are easier to pass.
Sometimes there is a food on the table you don't want. You can use thank you even when you say no.

blocks.name: et-scene

opts.readme: Read the question aloud, then let your child choose. Talk about why.
opts.prompt: Ruby doesn't like beans. What should she say?

choices.text: Ruby says, “No, thank you.”
choices.outcome: Grandma nods. No hurt feelings.

choices.text: Ruby says, “Yuck! Gross!”
choices.outcome: Grandma worked hard on those beans. Her feelings are hurt.

blocks.cap: Saying no kindly.

blocks.html: If you don't want a food, say “No, thank you” instead of “Yuck.”
Someone worked to make the food, and they can hear what we say. “No, thank you” says no without hurting feelings.
You can add something kind: “No, thank you. The rice is yummy, though!” The cook will be glad you liked part of the meal.

blocks.title: Let's practice
blocks.q: In Sam's family, everyone tries one small taste. Sam tries the carrots and doesn't like them. What does he say?
steps: Sam tried a small taste, like his family asks.
He doesn't want more.
He says so kindly.
blocks.a: “I tried it. No more, thank you.”

blocks.name: et-sort

cards.text: I tried it. No more, thank you.

cards.why: Say no, thank you instead.
The cook can see faces too.
Someone worked to make it.

opts.readme: Read each card aloud. Your child taps a card, then a group.

blocks.cap: Sort the cards: polite or not polite.

blocks.html: Making faces or saying “gross” about food on the table. The cook can hear it. A quiet “No, thank you” is enough, and many families ask for one small taste.
For the grown-up. Keep pressure low: offer, accept “No, thank you,” and offer again another day. Children often need many tries before they like a new food.
You started the meal together. When you are done, there is a polite way to leave the table too.

blocks.name: et-scene

opts.readme: Read the question aloud, then let your child choose. Talk about why.
opts.prompt: Leo is done. The others are still eating. What should he do?

choices.text: Leo asks, “May I please be excused?”
choices.outcome: Grandpa says yes. Leo thanks him and carries his plate.

choices.text: Leo jumps up and runs off to play.
choices.outcome: Grandpa looks up. Where did Leo go?

blocks.cap: Asking to be excused.

blocks.html: When you are done, ask “May I please be excused?”, thank the cook, and help carry your plate if you can.
Asking lets the family know you are done. Thanking the cook shows you noticed their work. Carrying your plate is a big help.
Different families do this in different ways. Some wait until everyone is done. Ask your grown-up what your family does.

blocks.title: Let's practice
blocks.q: Hana is done eating. Mom says, “Yes, you may.” What else can Hana do?
steps: Mom said yes.
Hana thanks her for dinner.
She carries her plate to the kitchen.
blocks.a: Hana says, “Thank you for dinner!” and carries her plate.

blocks.name: et-order

items: Wait for a grown-up to say yes.
Carry your plate to the kitchen.
opts.readme: Read the steps aloud. Your child taps two steps to swap them, then Check.
opts.title: Leaving the table

blocks.cap: Put the steps in order.

blocks.name: et-chart
blocks.cap: A table manners chart to print.

blocks.html: Leaving the table as soon as your own plate is empty. Asking to be excused lets the family know, and carrying a plate is a big help.
For the grown-up. Decide what “done” looks like for your family and say it simply. Show your child where to put their plate, and thank them every time they carry it.
A playdate at a friend's house is a treat. You already know how to say hello and share. A good guest does both.

blocks.name: et-scene

opts.readme: Read the question aloud, then let your child choose. Talk about why.
opts.prompt: Sam is thirsty at Ruby's house. What should he do?

choices.text: Sam asks, “May I please have some water?”
choices.outcome: Ruby's mom gets him a cup. Sam says thank you.

choices.text: Sam opens the fridge and takes a juice.
choices.outcome: That juice might have been for something special. In someone else's home, ask first.

blocks.cap: Asking first in someone else's home.

blocks.html: At a friend's house, greet the grown-ups, play nicely, ask before you open or take things, and help clean up before you go.
Another family's home is their space. Asking first and helping out shows respect, and it makes them glad to have you back.
If you are not sure about something at a friend's house, just ask a grown-up there: “Is it okay if I…?” Asking is always polite.

blocks.title: Let's practice
blocks.q: Hana arrives at Leo's house. Leo's dad opens the door. What should Hana do first?
steps: A grown-up opened the door.
Hana says hello to him first.
Then she says hi to Leo.
blocks.a: Hana says, “Hello! Thank you for having me.”

blocks.name: et-sort

cards.text: Hello! Thank you for having me.
May I please have some water?

cards.why: Ask first in someone else's home.
Ask a grown-up first.

opts.readme: Read each card aloud. Your child taps a card, then a group.

blocks.cap: Sort the cards: polite or not polite.

blocks.html: Opening closed doors, cabinets or the fridge at a friend's house. In someone else's home, ask first.
For the grown-up. Before a playdate, go over two or three simple rules: greet the grown-ups, ask before you take, help clean up. Afterward, ask the host how it went and praise what went well.
When a friend comes to your house, you are the host. You know how to be a good guest. Being a good host is the other side.

blocks.name: et-scene

opts.readme: Read the question aloud, then let your child choose. Talk about why.
opts.prompt: Omar has come to play. What should Mia say?

choices.text: Mia asks, “What do you want to play first?”
choices.outcome: Omar picks blocks. They build a castle together.

choices.text: Mia says, “We're playing my game. You watch.”
choices.outcome: Omar feels like he isn't welcome.

blocks.cap: Letting the guest choose.

blocks.html: A good host greets the guest at the door, lets the guest choose a game first, and walks them to the door at the end.
The host's job is to make the guest feel welcome. When the guest has fun, they want to come back.
Before your friend comes, you can plan two or three games to offer. Then let your guest pick which one to play first.

blocks.title: Let's practice
blocks.q: Sam's playdate at Ruby's house is over. What can Ruby do?
steps: The guest is leaving.
Ruby walks Sam to the door.
She says goodbye and thanks him for coming.
blocks.a: Ruby walks Sam to the door: “Thanks for coming!”

blocks.name: et-sort

cards.why: A host plays with the guest.
Put special things away before, then share the rest.

opts.readme: Read each card aloud. Your child taps a card, then a group.

blocks.cap: Sort the cards: good host or not.

blocks.html: Keeping favorite toys to yourself, or playing alone with a new game. The host's job is to make the guest feel welcome.
For the grown-up. Help your child plan: choose a few games together, and put away any toy that is too special to share. Remind them before the doorbell rings: “Your friend gets to pick first.”
Every home is a little different. A good guest notices how a family does things and follows along.

blocks.name: et-scene

opts.readme: Read the question aloud, then let your child choose. Talk about why.
opts.prompt: At Hana's house, everyone takes shoes off at the door. At Leo's house, people keep shoes on. What should Leo do?

choices.text: Leo takes his shoes off too.
choices.outcome: Hana's dad smiles. Leo is following their way.

choices.text: Leo says, “We don't have to do that at my house.”
choices.outcome: That is true at Leo's house. But at Hana's house, guests follow Hana's family's way.

blocks.cap: Following the host family's way.

blocks.html: Every family has its own rules, like shoes off at the door or no snacks on the couch. At their house, follow theirs.
A home belongs to the family who lives there. Following their rules shows respect and says thank you for having me.

blocks.title: Let's practice
blocks.q: At Sam's house, snacks are eaten at the table. At Mia's house, they can be eaten on the couch. Which family is right?
steps: Each family chose what works in its own home.
Neither way is wrong.
A guest follows the host family's way.
blocks.a: Both are right, each in its own home.

blocks.name: et-sort

cards.text: Taking shoes off when the family does
Eating snacks where the family eats them
“We don't do that at my house.”
cards.why: Each family's way is right for its home.
Respect the family's way.

opts.readme: Read each card aloud. Your child taps a card, then a group.

blocks.cap: Sort the cards: polite or not polite.

blocks.html: Saying “We don't have to do that at my house.” Each family's way is right for its own home, and guests follow the host's way.
Customs differ. Shoes on or off at the door, where snacks are eaten, how a meal starts: these differ from family to family and country to country. Respect every way; never laugh at one.
For the grown-up. Talk about your own family's rules and why you have them. When visiting, prompt your child to look for clues (shoes by the door) or simply to ask, “What is the rule here?”
A visit ends with goodbye. There is one more thing a good guest says before leaving.

blocks.name: et-scene

opts.readme: Read the question aloud, then let your child choose. Talk about why.
opts.prompt: Omar had fun at Mia's house. It is time to go. What should he do?

choices.text: Omar says to Mia's mom, “Thank you for having me!”
choices.outcome: Mia's mom smiles. Omar is welcome any time.

choices.text: Omar thanks Mia but forgets her mom.
choices.outcome: Close! Mia's mom made the playdate happen too.

blocks.cap: Thanking the grown-up host.

blocks.html: Before you leave a visit, find the grown-up and say “Thank you for having me.”
The grown-up host invited you, made snacks, and watched over you. A thank-you tells them you noticed.
If you went to a birthday party, you can say, “Thank you for the party!” If you slept over, you can say, “Thank you for having me over.”

blocks.title: Let's practice
blocks.q: Ruby's birthday party at Ruby's house is over. What can Leo say before he leaves?
steps: Ruby's family gave the party.
Leo finds Ruby's mom or dad.
He thanks them and says goodbye to Ruby.
blocks.a: “Thank you for having me! Happy birthday, Ruby!”

blocks.name: et-order

items: Look at them and say, “Thank you for having me!”
Walk out the door with your own grown-up.
opts.readme: Read the steps aloud. Your child taps two steps to swap them, then Check.
opts.title: Leaving a visit

blocks.cap: Put the steps in order.

blocks.html: Thanking the friend but forgetting the grown-up who hosted. The parent made the playdate happen too.
For the grown-up. Arrive a minute early at pickup so your child has time to find the host. In the car, say how proud you are when they remember on their own.
A line is taking turns with lots of people. We find lines at the slide, at lunch, and at the store.

blocks.name: et-scene

opts.readme: Read the question aloud, then let your child choose. Talk about why.
opts.prompt: There is a line for the slide. Sam just got there. His friend Hana is near the front. What should Sam do?

choices.text: Sam goes to the end of the line.
choices.outcome: Everyone waits their turn. It is fair.

choices.text: Sam cuts in to stand with Hana.
choices.outcome: Leo was waiting. Cutting in to stand with a friend is still cutting.

blocks.cap: Going to the end of the line.

blocks.html: In a line: go to the end, wait your turn, keep your hands to yourself, and don't cut.
Everyone in the line is waiting too. Going in order is fair, and fair feels good.
Waiting can feel long. You can count, hum quietly, or look around for something blue. Your turn will come.

blocks.title: Let's practice
blocks.q: Mia is in line for lunch. Her friend Omar is not here yet. Should she save him a spot?
steps: Omar is not in the line.
Saving him a spot puts him ahead of people who were waiting.
That is cutting too.
blocks.a: No. Omar goes to the end when he comes.

blocks.name: et-sort

cards.text: Going to the end of the line

cards.why: Wait your turn.
That is still cutting.

cards.text: Saving a spot for someone not there
cards.why: That is cutting too.

opts.readme: Read each card aloud. Your child taps a card, then a group.

blocks.cap: Sort the cards: polite or not polite.

blocks.html: Cutting in to stand with a friend, or pushing to get closer. Saving a spot for someone who is not there is cutting too.
For the grown-up. Lines are boring for little ones. Play quiet games while you wait: I spy, counting colors, or guessing what is next. Praise patient waiting out loud.
At the store we wait in lines and use an inside voice. There are a few more store manners too.

blocks.name: et-scene

opts.readme: Read the question aloud, then let your child choose. Talk about why.
opts.prompt: Ruby sees a toy she wants. Dad says, “Not today.” What should Ruby do?

choices.text: Ruby says, “Okay,” and helps push the cart.
choices.outcome: Dad says thank you. Shopping is easy when Ruby takes no for an answer.

choices.text: Ruby cries and shouts, “I WANT IT!”
choices.outcome: Other shoppers turn to look. It is hard for Dad to shop.

blocks.cap: Taking no for an answer at the store.

blocks.html: At the store: stay close to your grown-up, use a quiet voice, touch only what you plan to buy, and say thank you to the cashier.
The store's things belong to the store. Other shoppers are busy. Staying close and calm helps everyone, and keeps you from getting lost.
It helps to have a job at the store, like holding the list or finding the bread. Helping makes the time go fast.

blocks.title: Let's practice
blocks.q: The cashier hands Omar the bag. What does Omar say?
steps: The cashier helped Omar and his grown-up.
People at work like to be thanked too.
Omar says so.
blocks.a: “Thank you!”

blocks.name: et-sort

cards.text: Saying thank you to the cashier
Asking once, and taking no for an answer
Opening a box to look inside
cards.why: Touch only what you plan to buy.
Other shoppers could get bumped.

opts.readme: Read each card aloud. Your child taps a card, then a group.

blocks.cap: Sort the cards: polite or not polite.

blocks.html: Opening packages, running in the aisles, or begging loudly for treats. The store belongs to other people, and other shoppers are busy.

For the grown-up. Before you go in, say the plan: “We are buying milk and bread. No treats today.” Give your child a job, like holding the list or finding the bread. Thank them for good store manners on the way out.
The library is full of books for everyone to share. It is a place for an inside voice, and even softer.

blocks.name: et-scene

opts.readme: Read the question aloud, then let your child choose. Talk about why.
say: Please put books on the cart.
opts.prompt: Leo is done with a book. What should he do?

choices.text: Leo puts the book on the cart.
choices.outcome: The librarian will put it back in just the right spot.

choices.text: Leo pushes it into any empty spot on a shelf.
choices.outcome: Now the next reader may never find it! The librarian asked for the cart.

blocks.cap: Putting books where the librarian asks.

blocks.html: At the library: use a whisper voice, handle books gently, and put books where the librarian asks.
Other people are reading and thinking. Library books belong to everyone, so we keep them nice for the next reader.
Your library card lets you take books home. Keep them in a safe spot, and bring them back on time so other kids can read them too.

blocks.title: Let's practice
blocks.q: Hana wants to tell Sam about a funny book. They are at the library. How should she talk?
steps: They are at the library.
Other people are reading.
Hana uses the softest voice.
blocks.a: Hana whispers.

blocks.name: et-sort

cards.why: Use a bookmark.
Whisper in the library.

opts.readme: Read each card aloud. Your child taps a card, then a group.

blocks.cap: Sort the cards: polite or not polite.

blocks.html: Putting books back in any empty spot. Many libraries ask you to leave books on a cart, so they go back in the right place.
For the grown-up. Give your child a bookmark of their own, and a special bag for library books. At home, keep library books in one spot so they come back clean and on time.
The library is one quiet place. There are others: a concert, a play, a waiting room, a place of worship.

blocks.name: et-scene

opts.readme: Read the question aloud, then let your child choose. Talk about why.
opts.prompt: Mia is at a concert with Grandma. The music is playing. Mia wants to say something. What should she do?

choices.text: Mia waits until the music stops, then whispers.
choices.outcome: Everyone hears the whole song.

choices.text: Mia whispers during the song.
choices.outcome: Even a whisper can be heard during quiet music. It can wait for the break.

blocks.cap: Waiting for a break to talk.

blocks.html: In quiet places, sit still, keep your voice low or silent, and follow the place's customs.
Everyone came to listen, to rest, or to think. Being quiet lets everyone enjoy it.

blocks.title: Let's practice
blocks.q: Sam visits a place of worship with Ruby's family. Everyone is quiet. What should Sam do?
steps: Sam doesn't know this place's customs.
He watches Ruby's family.
He sits quietly and follows what they do. Questions can wait until after.
blocks.a: Sam sits quietly and follows Ruby's family.

blocks.name: et-sort

cards.why: Even whispers wait for a break.
The person in front can feel it.

opts.readme: Read each card aloud. Your child taps a card, then a group.

blocks.cap: Sort the cards: polite or not polite.

blocks.html: Thinking whispering is fine during a performance or a service. In most quiet places, even whispers wait for a break.
Customs differ. Every place of worship and every performance has its own customs: when to stand, when to sit, when to clap. When you visit, watch your hosts and follow along.

For the grown-up. Before a quiet event, say what will happen and how long it lasts. Bring a quiet activity for waiting rooms. Plan a signal (a squeeze of the hand) for “I need to tell you something at the break.”
The doctor's office is a quiet place where people help us stay healthy. Manners help there too.

blocks.name: et-scene

opts.readme: Read the question aloud, then let your child choose. Talk about why.
say: How are you feeling today, Omar?
opts.prompt: Dr. Bell asks Omar a question. He feels a little nervous. What can he do?

choices.text: Omar answers as well as he can, and Mom helps.
choices.outcome: Dr. Bell listens. It is fine to feel nervous; Mom is right there.

choices.text: Omar says, “Go away!”
choices.outcome: Dr. Bell wants to help. A kind answer is better, even a quiet one.

blocks.cap: Answering the doctor's questions.

blocks.html: At the doctor's office: wait calmly, answer the doctor's questions, and say thank you when the visit is over.
Answering helps the doctor and nurse take care of us. Waiting calmly is kind to the other people who are waiting.
Doctors and nurses are there to help. It is okay to say, “I'm scared.” They hear that a lot, and they will explain what they are doing.

blocks.title: Let's practice
blocks.q: The visit with Dr. Bell is over. What does Hana say?
steps: Dr. Bell helped Hana today.
Hana looks at her.
She says thank you.
blocks.a: “Thank you, Dr. Bell!”

blocks.html: Hiding or refusing to talk to the doctor or nurse. It is fine to feel nervous. Your grown-up stays with you and can help answer.
For the grown-up. Play doctor at home with a toy kit, taking turns. Tell your child what will happen at the visit in simple, honest words, and bring a favorite book for the waiting room.
Doors are everywhere: at school, at the store, at home. Here is a small kindness that takes one second. It is like waiting in line: we think about the person behind us.

blocks.name: et-scene

opts.readme: Read the question aloud, then let your child choose. Talk about why.
opts.prompt: Grandpa is right behind Hana, with his hands full. What should Hana do?

choices.text: Hana looks back and holds the door for Grandpa.
choices.outcome: Grandpa walks right through.

choices.text: Hana lets the door swing shut.
choices.outcome: Grandpa has to stop and juggle his bags.

blocks.cap: Holding the door.

blocks.html: Look behind you when you go through a door, and hold it for anyone close behind, especially someone with full hands.
A door that swings shut can bump the next person. Holding it is a small kindness that helps a lot.
Holding a door is also kind for a friend in a wheelchair, someone pushing a stroller, or a person carrying a big box.

blocks.title: Let's practice
blocks.q: Ms. Park holds the door open for Leo. What does Leo do?
steps: Someone helped Leo.
He goes through.
He says thank you.
blocks.a: Leo says, “Thank you, Ms. Park!”

blocks.html: Letting a door swing shut on the person behind you. A quick look back is the whole trick.
For the grown-up. Make it a game: who can be the family's “door helper” today? Hold doors for your child too, and say “You're welcome” when they thank you.
Coughs and sneezes happen to everyone. Just like washing hands, covering them keeps germs from spreading to other people.

blocks.name: et-scene

opts.readme: Read the question aloud, then let your child choose. Talk about why.
opts.prompt: Sam has to sneeze. There is no tissue. What should he do?

choices.text: Sam turns away and sneezes into his elbow.
choices.outcome: Mia stays dry, and Sam's hands stay cleaner.

choices.text: Sam sneezes into his open hand, then picks up the crayons.
choices.outcome: Now the germs are on the crayons everyone uses. The elbow is the better spot.

blocks.cap: Sneezing into the elbow.

blocks.html: Cough or sneeze into a tissue or your elbow, turn away from people and food, and wash or clean your hands after.
Coughs and sneezes spray tiny drops. Covering them keeps the drops off other people, food and the things everyone touches.
If you feel a sneeze coming, you have a second or two. Turn your head away and lift your elbow. That is all it takes.

blocks.title: Let's practice
blocks.q: Ruby has a tissue and needs to cough. What does she do?
steps: She coughs into the tissue.
She throws the tissue in the trash.
She washes her hands.
blocks.a: Tissue, trash, wash.

blocks.name: et-order

items: Turn away from people and food.
Throw the tissue in the trash.
opts.readme: Read the steps aloud. Your child taps two steps to swap them, then Check.
opts.title: Covering a cough

blocks.cap: Put the steps in order.

blocks.name: et-sort

cards.why: Then the germs go on everything you touch.
Turn away and cover it.

opts.readme: Read each card aloud. Your child taps a card, then a group.

blocks.cap: Sort the cards: good way or not.

blocks.name: et-chart
blocks.cap: A chart to print.

blocks.html: Coughing into an open hand and then touching things others use. The inside of the elbow is the better spot when there is no tissue.
For the grown-up. Practice “elbow sneezes” as a silly game, so it becomes a reflex. Keep tissues where little hands can reach them, and a trash can nearby.

sources.name: CDC, “Coughing and Sneezing”: cover with a tissue or your upper sleeve, throw the tissue away, wash your hands

blocks.html: After we share and play, the toys are everywhere. Then it is time to tidy up.

blocks.name: et-scene

opts.readme: Read the question aloud, then let your child choose. Talk about why.
opts.prompt: Playtime at Ruby's house is over. Omar helped make the mess. What should they do?

choices.text: Ruby and Omar tidy up together.
choices.outcome: With two helpers, it is done in no time.

choices.text: Ruby says, “Omar made the mess, so he cleans up.”
choices.outcome: They both played. Everyone who played helps tidy.

blocks.cap: Tidying up together.

blocks.html: When we finish playing, we put toys back where they belong. Everyone who played helps.
Tidying keeps toys safe and easy to find next time. Helping together is fair, and it is faster.
A good trick is to tidy as you go. When you finish with one toy, put it away before you take out the next one.

blocks.title: Let's practice
blocks.q: Leo plays with blocks at Mia's house. It is almost time to go. What should Leo do?
steps: Leo played with the blocks too.
They belong in the bin.
He helps Mia put them away before he goes.
blocks.a: Leo helps Mia put the blocks in the bin.

blocks.name: et-order

items: Put the bin on the shelf.
opts.readme: Read the steps aloud. Your child taps two steps to swap them, then Check.
opts.title: Tidying up

blocks.cap: Put the tidy-up steps in order.

blocks.name: et-chart
blocks.cap: A chart to print. Star each day your child tidies without being asked twice.

blocks.html: Leaving the cleanup to the grown-ups or to whoever owns the toys. Everyone who played helps tidy.

For the grown-up. Use a clean-up song and a timer: “Can we beat the song?” Give simple jobs (“You do the red blocks, I'll do the blue”) and a place for everything, with pictures on bins for non-readers.
You have learned many kind words. Here is the biggest idea of all: manners are about how other people feel.

blocks.name: et-scene

opts.readme: Read the question aloud, then let your child choose. Talk about why.
opts.prompt: Hana is sitting alone. She looks sad. What can Leo do?

choices.text: Leo asks, “Are you okay? Do you want to play with us?”
choices.outcome: Hana smiles and joins in. Leo noticed.

choices.text: Leo walks by without looking.
choices.outcome: Hana still sits alone.

blocks.cap: Noticing a friend who looks sad.

blocks.html: Notice when someone is sad, left out or hurt. Ask, “Are you okay?” or invite them in.
Please and thank you are words. But the heart of good manners is caring how people feel, and doing something kind about it.
Faces and bodies can tell us how someone feels. A frown, tears, or sitting alone can mean someone needs a friend.

blocks.title: Let's practice
blocks.q: Mia falls down and starts to cry. What can Omar do?
steps: Omar notices that Mia is hurt.
He asks if she is okay.
He gets a grown-up to help.
blocks.a: Omar asks, “Are you okay?” and gets a grown-up.

blocks.name: et-sort

cards.text: Getting a grown-up when someone is hurt

cards.why: It hurts to be laughed at.

cards.text: Walking past someone who is crying
cards.why: Stop and ask if they are okay.

opts.readme: Read each card aloud. Your child taps a card, then a group.

blocks.cap: Sort the cards: kind or not kind.

blocks.html: Thinking manners are only words to say. Noticing someone who looks sad, and being kind to them, is the heart of good manners.

For the grown-up. Name feelings as they happen, in books and in life: “How do you think the bear feels?” Notice and praise kindness more than politeness: “You saw Hana was alone and asked her to play. That was kind.”
Getting a gift is exciting! You know to say thank you. Opening a gift kindly takes one more step.

blocks.name: et-scene

opts.readme: Read the question aloud, then let your child choose. Talk about why.
opts.prompt: Sam opens a gift from Grandma June. It is a book he already has. What should he say?

choices.text: Sam says, “Thank you, Grandma! I love this book.”
choices.outcome: Grandma smiles. She is glad she picked a book Sam loves.

choices.text: Sam says, “I already have this.”
choices.outcome: Grandma feels sad. She chose it just for Sam.

blocks.cap: Thanking the giver.

blocks.html: When you open a gift, look at the giver, say thank you, and say something kind, even if it is not what you hoped for.
The giver thought about you and chose the gift for you. Thank you tells them you are glad they thought of you.

blocks.title: Let's practice
blocks.q: Ruby gives Leo socks for his birthday. Leo hoped for a toy. What can he say that is kind and true?
steps: Leo is a little surprised.
Ruby chose the socks for him.
He thanks her for thinking of him.
blocks.a: “Thank you for thinking of me, Ruby!”

blocks.name: et-sort

cards.text: Thank you for thinking of me.

cards.why: Thank them for thinking of you instead.

cards.text: (Tosses it aside for the next gift.)
cards.why: Each giver gets a thank-you.
The giver chose it for you.

opts.readme: Read each card aloud. Your child taps a card, then a group.

blocks.cap: Sort the cards: kind or not kind.

blocks.html: Saying “I already have this” or tossing a gift aside to open the next one. The giver chose it for you; thank them for thinking of you.

For the grown-up. Practice with wrapped household objects (a spoon, a sock) and let your child practice a gracious “Thank you!” It is silly, and it works. Open gifts slowly at parties, one giver at a time.
After you open a gift or someone does something kind for you, you can send a thank-you of your very own.

blocks.name: et-scene

opts.readme: Read the question aloud, then let your child choose. Talk about why.
opts.prompt: Grandma gave Mia a kite. Mia wants to say thank you. What can she make?

choices.text: A picture of the kite, “Thank you for the kite!” and her name.
choices.outcome: Grandma will love it. It is short and from the heart.

choices.text: Nothing. Mia thinks a thank-you note must be long and hard.
choices.outcome: A few words and a picture make a perfect thank-you.

blocks.cap: Making a thank-you picture.

blocks.html: Draw a picture, write a few thank-you words, and sign your name.
A thank-you picture lasts. The giver can keep it, and it shows you took time to thank them.
Grown-ups love getting mail. You can put your picture in an envelope and mail it, or hand it to the giver the next time you see them.

blocks.title: Let's practice
blocks.q: Uncle Kofi gave Omar a ball. What could Omar's thank-you picture say?
steps: Draw the ball, or Omar playing with it.
Write: “Thank you for the ball! I kick it every day!”
Sign: “Love, Omar.”
blocks.a: “Thank you for the ball! I kick it every day! Love, Omar”

blocks.name: et-note

parts.thanks: Thank you for the kite! I flew it at the park!

blocks.cap: A thank-you picture has three parts: a picture, the thank-you words and your name.

blocks.name: et-order

items: Draw your picture and write your thank-you words.
Sign your name at the end.
Give or mail it to the giver.
opts.readme: Read the steps aloud. Your child taps two steps to swap them, then Check.
opts.title: Making a thank-you picture

blocks.cap: Put the steps in order.

blocks.html: Thinking a thank-you note must be long. “Thank you for the kite. I flew it at the park! Love, Mia” is a perfect note.

For the grown-up. Keep paper, crayons and envelopes in one place. Very young children can draw while you write their words; older ones can copy or write their own. Mailing it together is part of the fun.
